design_note: Each eval targets a post-training-cutoff knowledge delta (Swift 6.2-6.4), not reasoning ability. A competent model without the skill gives a confidently wrong answer from stale knowledge. Expectations grade two objective dimensions: correct version gate (which Swift/compiler) and correct deployment-target story (language feature vs OS-gated runtime API). Runner rule: executors must not use web search or documentation MCP tools, so the measured delta is the skill's contribution.

evals.name: defer-await-cleanup
evals.prompt: We just moved our project to Xcode 27 (Swift 6.4). I have an async function that opens a network connection and I need `await connection.close()` to run on every exit path, including early throws. Our deployment target is still iOS 17. What's the cleanest way to guarantee that cleanup?
evals.expected_output: Recommends await directly inside defer (SE-0493), notes it works on any deployment target, rejects the Task-in-defer workaround
expectations: Recommends `defer { await connection.close() }` as the primary solution (await directly inside defer)
States that await-in-defer is a Swift 6.4 language feature usable regardless of deployment target (iOS 17 is fine)
Does not recommend `defer { Task { ... } }` as the solution (or explicitly rejects it as an anti-pattern)

evals.name: cancellation-shield-availability
evals.prompt: I read that Swift now lets you ignore task cancellation while running cleanup. Can I use withTaskCancellationShield in our app? We support iOS 18 and newer. If not, what should I do instead when a cancelled task keeps skipping my cleanup code?
evals.expected_output: Confirms the API exists (SE-0504, Swift 6.4), states the iOS 27+ runtime gate, offers pre-27 fallback
expectations: Correctly identifies withTaskCancellationShield as a real API (SE-0504 / Swift 6.4), not a hallucination or unknown
States it requires iOS 27+ / macOS 27+ (or aligned tvOS/watchOS/visionOS releases) at runtime and therefore cannot be used unconditionally with an iOS 18 deployment target
Offers a working pre-iOS-27 alternative such as `await Task { ... }.value` to break out of the task tree, or #available-gated adoption

evals.name: throwing-task-warning
evals.prompt: After updating to Xcode 27, I'm getting warnings like 'unstructured throwing task created by init(name:priority:operation:) is not used, which may accidentally ignore errors thrown inside the task' all over our codebase. What changed, and what's the right way to fix these? Some of them are fire-and-forget analytics uploads where we genuinely don't care about failures.
evals.expected_output: Identifies SE-0520 (@discardableResult removed from throwing Task inits in Swift 6.4) and gives ranked fixes
expectations: Explains the cause: Swift 6.4 removed @discardableResult from throwing Task/Task.detached initializers (SE-0520)
Recommends handling errors inside the task or storing/awaiting the task value as the primary fixes
For genuine fire-and-forget cases, recommends explicit discard (`_ = Task { ... }`) or do/catch inside the closure — not removing `try` or globally suppressing the diagnostic

evals.name: weak-let-sendable
evals.prompt: I have `final class ConnectionPool: Sendable` and need a weak back-reference to its owning coordinator. The compiler historically forced weak properties to be var, which breaks Sendable conformance. Is there a way to do this now without resorting to @unchecked Sendable? We're on the Swift 6.3 toolchain (Xcode 26.6).
evals.expected_output: weak let since Swift 6.3 (SE-0481), no flag or OS gate for declarations
expectations: States that `weak let` is legal since Swift 6.3 (SE-0481) and solves exactly this problem
Does not claim weak let declarations require a feature flag or a minimum OS version
Shows or describes the weak let stored property pattern inside a Sendable class

evals.name: nonisolated-async-isolation
evals.prompt: In our app (Xcode 27 project, Approachable Concurrency enabled, Swift 6 language mode), I have `class ImageProcessor { func process(_ data: Data) async -> UIImage }` — no isolation annotations. When I call it from a @MainActor view model, which thread does process() run on? It's doing heavy decoding and I think it's blocking the UI. How do I fix it?
evals.expected_output: With NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault the method inherits the caller's actor (MainActor); fix with @concurrent
expectations: States that with Approachable Concurrency (NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault), the nonisolated async method inherits the caller's isolation and runs on the MainActor in this scenario
Recommends @concurrent as the primary way to move the work to the generic executor (not Task.detached)
Notes that the answer depends on the NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault / Approachable Concurrency setting rather than being unconditional

evals.name: task-immediate-availability
evals.prompt: Is Task.immediate just a compiler-level feature? We build with the latest Xcode but still deploy to iOS 17. I want to use it in a gesture handler so the first part of the work happens synchronously before the runloop hop. Will that work on iOS 17 devices?
evals.expected_output: SE-0472, Swift 6.2 compiler but iOS 26+ runtime gate — not usable unconditionally on iOS 17
expectations: Correctly identifies Task.immediate as a real API (SE-0472, shipped with Swift 6.2)
States it is runtime-gated to iOS 26+ / macOS 26+ (or aligned tvOS/watchOS/visionOS releases) and will not run unconditionally on iOS 17 — availability handling required
Explains the distinction between compiler-only language features (any deployment target) and runtime-gated APIs (minimum OS), applying it to this case
